name: Sydney
description: Australia's biggest city wraps around a harbour of beaches, ferries and sandstone headlands. Easy to reach, easy to explore on foot.
funFacts: The sails of the Sydney Opera House are covered in more than one million tiles.
Locals call the Sydney Harbour Bridge "the Coathanger".

image.alt: Sydney Opera House on the harbour

name: Cairns
description: A tropical gateway city in Far North Queensland, and the usual base for reef trips and the Daintree rainforest.
funFacts: Cairns sits between two World Heritage areas: the Great Barrier Reef and the Wet Tropics rainforest.
The nearby Daintree Rainforest is estimated to be around 180 million years old.

image.alt: Central Cairns with the ranges behind

name: Darwin
description: The tropical capital of the Northern Territory and the starting point for Kakadu and the Top End.
funFacts: Darwin was bombed by Japanese aircraft on 19 February 1942, the largest attack ever made on Australia.
Cyclone Tracy destroyed most of the city on Christmas Eve 1974, and Darwin was rebuilt.

image.alt: The Darwin skyline across the harbour

name: Alice Springs
description: The main town of the Red Centre, set among the MacDonnell Ranges and a long way from anywhere else.
funFacts: Alice Springs lies close to the geographic centre of Australia.
The Ghan train stops here on its Adelaide to Darwin journey.

image.alt: Anzac Hill above Alice Springs

name: Uluru
description: The great sandstone monolith of Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, a sacred place for the Anangu people.
funFacts: Uluru stands 348 metres high and is about 9.4 kilometres around its base.
Climbing Uluru was permanently closed on 26 October 2019.

image.alt: Uluru glowing red in the desert

name: Great Barrier Reef
description: The outer reef, reached by boat from Cairns, Port Douglas or the Whitsundays. Snorkelling and diving at their best.
funFacts: It is the world's largest coral reef system, stretching about 2,300 kilometres along the Queensland coast.
The reef is made up of around 2,900 individual reefs.

image.alt: Coral on the Great Barrier Reef

name: Great Ocean Road
description: A winding coastal road in Victoria with surf beaches, cliffs and the Twelve Apostles limestone stacks.
funFacts: The road was built by returned soldiers after World War I and is a memorial to those who died in the war.
Construction began in 1919 and the road opened in 1932.
access: About 275 km west of Melbourne, roughly a four-hour drive along the Great Ocean Road
tip: Bookings are essential to secure parking at the Twelve Apostles. Start at the Keerray Woorroong Visitor Centre.

image.alt: The Twelve Apostles on the Great Ocean Road

name: Perth
description: A sunny Indian Ocean city on the Swan River, with white beaches and Rottnest Island just offshore.
funFacts: Perth is one of the most isolated major cities in the world.
Rottnest Island, a short ferry ride away, is home to the quokka.

image.alt: Elizabeth Quay Bridge in Perth

name: Yulara
description: The village at the edge of Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park, and the usual base for visiting Uluru and Kata Tjuta.
funFacts: Kata Tjuta is about 50 km by road from Uluru.
The Curtin Springs roadhouse is approximately 100 km from Yulara.

image.alt: Uluru seen from the Naninga Lookout at Yulara

name: Uluru Base Walk
access: Starts at the Mala car park
description: A loop around the whole base of Uluru, with water and toilets. The park recommends starting early from the Mala car park and walking clockwise.
funFacts: Some tracks at Uluru close in the afternoon during summer because of the high risk of heat stroke.

trail.name: Uluru Base Walk
trail.note: In hot weather, walk only in the cooler morning hours and finish before 11 am.

tip: Short on time? The Mala Walk is 2 km return (about 1.5 hours) and the Kuniya Walk is 1 km return (30 to 45 minutes). Both start at the base.

image.alt: The base of Uluru seen from the Kuniya Walk

name: Talinguru Nyakunytjaku
description: The main sunrise viewing area for Uluru, with water and toilets.
funFacts: Two short loops start here: the Minymaku (Women's) walk is 1 km (30 minutes) and the Watiku (Men's) walk is 1.5 km (45 minutes).
tip: Both loops are wheelchair accessible, so they work for prams and slower walkers.

image.alt: Visitors at the Uluru sunrise viewing area

name: Walpa Gorge Walk
access: Kata Tjuta is about 50 km by road from Uluru
description: A walk into the gorge between the domes of Kata Tjuta. There is water at the start but no toilets.

image.alt: Reflections in Walpa Gorge, Kata Tjuta

name: Valley of the Winds
access: Kata Tjuta is about 50 km by road from Uluru
description: The longer walk among the domes of Kata Tjuta. It is steep, rocky and difficult in places.

trail.name: Valley of the Winds loop
trail.note: The walk closes at the first lookout (Karu) from 11 am when the forecast or actual temperature reaches 36°C or more.

tip: No time for the full loop? The Karu lookout is 2.2 km return (about 1 hour) and the Karingana lookout is 5.4 km return (about 2.5 hours).

sources.name: Parks Australia: Valley of the Winds walks

image.alt: Valley of the Winds at Kata Tjuta

name: Kings Canyon
access: About 450 km south-west of Alice Springs, roughly 4 hours' drive
description: The sandstone canyon in Watarrka National Park, a long drive from Alice Springs or Uluru.

sources.name: Tourism NT: Kings Canyon Rim Walk

image.alt: View over Kings Canyon

name: Kings Canyon Rim Walk
description: A loop along the top of the canyon walls in Watarrka National Park.

trail.name: Rim Walk
trail.note: On days forecast to reach 36°C or more you have to start early in the morning. Check the current cut-off time with the park on the day.

sources.name: Tourism NT: Kings Canyon Rim Walk
NT Parks: short walks in Watarrka

image.alt: The Rim Walk above Kings Canyon
image.credit: David Ashford from Dublin, Ireland / Wikimedia Commons

name: Simpsons Gap
description: A gap in the West MacDonnell Ranges with several short walks. Sections 1 and 2 of the Larapinta Trail start here.

image.alt: Simpsons Gap in the West MacDonnell Ranges

name: Standley Chasm
description: A narrow chasm in the West MacDonnell Ranges, reached by a well-maintained trail.

image.alt: The narrow walls of Standley Chasm

name: Ormiston Gorge
description: A gorge with a large waterhole in the West MacDonnell Ranges. The Pound Walk starts at the visitor centre and returns past the main waterhole.

image.alt: Ormiston Gorge

name: Ellery Creek Big Hole
description: A waterhole in the West MacDonnell Ranges, reached by a gravel road that is suitable for two-wheel drive vehicles.
tip: The Dolomite walk here is 3 km.

sources.name: Tourism NT: Ellery Creek Big Hole

image.alt: Ellery Creek Big Hole waterhole

name: Wentworth Falls
description: A lookout and short walk to the falls in the Blue Mountains. The track has hidden cliff edges and many steep stairs.

trail.name: Wentworth Falls track
trail.note: Not suitable for prams and no wheelchair access.

sources.name: NSW National Parks: Wentworth Falls track

image.alt: Wentworth Falls in the Blue Mountains
image.credit: Alex Proimos from Sydney, Australia / Wikimedia Commons

name: National Pass
description: A loop below the cliffs at Wentworth Falls with many steep stairs and hidden cliff edges. Mobile reception is limited.

trail.name: National Pass
trail.note: The park page lists a closure between Valley of the Waters and Slacks Stairs because of rockfall, and some sections can become impassable after rain. Check the current status before you go.

image.alt: The National Pass track in the Blue Mountains

name: Grand Canyon Track
description: A canyon walk at Blackheath in the Blue Mountains. There is no drinking water at the location.

trail.name: Grand Canyon Track
trail.note: The creek can flood after heavy rain. The park says never to walk in a canyon before, during or after heavy rain.

sources.name: NSW National Parks: Grand Canyon track

image.alt: The Grand Canyon Track at Blackheath
image.credit: Andrea Schaffer from Sydney, Australia / Wikimedia Commons

name: Royal National Park Coast Track
access: By train on the Cronulla line, then the ferry to Bundeena and a 1.5 km walk to the track start
description: The coast track from Bundeena to Otford is a two-day walk. There is no drinking water on the track, and the water at Wattamolla and Garie Beach is not drinkable.

trail.name: The Coast Track (Bundeena to Otford)
trail.note: Bring at least 2 litres of water per person per day. The beaches are not patrolled and can have strong rips. Total fire bans may apply, and the park can close for poor weather or fire danger.

tip: Shorter option from Bundeena: the Bundeena Drive to Marley walk is 7.8 km return, 3 to 4 hours (Grade 3).

sources.name: NSW National Parks: The Coast Track
NSW National Parks: Bundeena Drive to Marley walk

image.alt: The Coast Track in Royal National Park

name: West Head
description: The West Head lookout in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park, with the Aboriginal Heritage walk past rock art. Bring drinking water.

trail.name: Aboriginal Heritage walk
trail.note: The rock art is delicate, so do not touch it. The gates to West Head close at 8.30 pm in daylight saving time and at 6 pm the rest of the year, and open at 6 am.

sources.name: NSW National Parks: Aboriginal Heritage walk
NSW National Parks: West Head lookout

image.alt: West Head in Ku-ring-gai Chase National Park

name: Melbourne
description: Victoria's capital, and the usual base for day trips to the Dandenong Ranges, Phillip Island, Wilsons Promontory and the Mornington Peninsula.
funFacts: The Twelve Apostles are about 275 km west of Melbourne, roughly a four-hour drive along the Great Ocean Road.
Phillip Island's Penguin Parade is about 90 minutes' drive from Melbourne.

sources.name: Phillip Island Nature Parks: Penguin Parade

image.alt: The Melbourne skyline

name: Dandenong Ranges
access: The 1000 Steps walk starts at the Ferntree Gully Picnic Area; the train station is about 1.2 km away
description: Dandenong Ranges National Park, home of the 1000 Steps Kokoda Memorial Walk. You complete the loop by taking the Lyrebird Track back to the car park.

trail.name: 1000 Steps Kokoda Memorial Walk
trail.note: The park closes on days of Extreme Fire Danger Rating or severe weather. The car park is usually full by 10 am on weekend mornings.

image.alt: Forest in the Dandenong Ranges

name: Penguin Parade
access: About 90 minutes' drive from Melbourne, plus around 20 minutes from the bridge
description: Little penguins come ashore at Phillip Island at sunset, any night of the year. Bookings are essential.
tip: Arrive about an hour before the penguins. There are no return buses from the Parade, and drivers should take care at dawn, dusk and night.

sources.name: Phillip Island Nature Parks: Penguin Parade

image.alt: The Penguin Parade at Phillip Island

name: Squeaky Beach
access: Wilsons Promontory is approximately three hours' drive from Melbourne
description: A beach in Wilsons Promontory National Park, reached by a walk the park calls suitable for all levels, including strollers.
tip: Swimming is not recommended because of persistent rips, and the beach is not patrolled. The car park is limited and fills quickly.

image.alt: The coast near Squeaky Beach in Wilsons Promontory National Park

name: Mount Oberon Walk
access: Starts at the Telegraph Saddle car park in Wilsons Promontory
description: A walk to a summit in Wilsons Promontory National Park. The final 100 m is a steep climb of timber and granite steps.

trail.name: Mount Oberon Walk
trail.note: Beware of unprotected cliffs. Granite boulders may be slippery when wet.

image.alt: Mount Oberon in Wilsons Promontory

name: Point Nepean
access: 110 km south of Melbourne, near Portsea
description: Point Nepean National Park has the Bay Beach Walk, the Range Area Walk and the Coles Track, which is shared with cyclists.
tip: Snakes are common in the warmer months, there is no drinking water beyond the Quarantine Station, and the bay beach can have strong currents and rips.

sources.name: Parks Victoria: Point Nepean National Park

image.alt: Point Nepean at the entrance to Port Phillip Bay

name: Mornington Peninsula
description: Mornington Peninsula National Park. Ocean beaches have dangerous undertows, rips and large swells, and the cliffs are unstable, so keep to marked trails.

trail.name: Two Bays Walking Trail
trail.note: A hike from Dromana to Cape Schanck.

sources.name: Parks Victoria: Mornington Peninsula National Park

image.alt: Cape Schanck Lighthouse
image.credit: Steve Bittinger from Canberra, Australia / Wikimedia Commons

name: Loch Ard Gorge
access: Just three minutes west of the Twelve Apostles
description: A gorge on the Great Ocean Road with trails to lookouts. Accessible parking serves the Geology and Loch Ard lookout trails.

image.alt: Loch Ard Gorge on the Great Ocean Road

name: Healesville Sanctuary
description: A wildlife sanctuary run by Zoos Victoria, open daily from 9 am to 5 pm.

image.alt: A short-beaked echidna at Healesville Sanctuary
